title: Mitral Valve Prolapse: Confirm the Lesion, Reassure the Low-Risk Patient, Refer Significant MR
bottomLine: Mitral valve prolapse is usually benign when isolated, but the clinical question is whether there is significant mitral regurgitation, arrhythmia, ventricular change or a syndromic/family-risk context. Confirm with echocardiography when indicated and avoid routine antibiotic prophylaxis or activity restriction in low-risk disease.
recognize: A midsystolic click with or without late systolic murmur can suggest MVP; symptoms such as palpitations or atypical chest discomfort are nonspecific.
Risk rises when substantial MR, LV/LA enlargement, AF, ventricular arrhythmia or family history of sudden cardiac death is present.
differentiate: MVP itself is not the same as severe MR.
Palpitations in MVP still require rhythm documentation rather than being attributed automatically to the valve.
assessment: Assess exertional dyspnea, palpitations/syncope, murmur characteristics, family history, connective-tissue features and prior echo findings.
Review pregnancy plans and prior endocarditis or valve intervention.
workup: Use echocardiography to confirm valve morphology and quantify MR when clinical findings warrant it.
Use rhythm monitoring if symptoms suggest arrhythmia; repeat echo according to MR severity and clinical change rather than an arbitrary annual schedule.
management: Reassure isolated low-risk MVP and manage cardiovascular risk normally.
Refer significant MR, LV changes, AF, recurrent syncope or complex ventricular arrhythmia to cardiology/structural-heart care.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe antibiotic prophylaxis solely for MVP without a current high-risk endocarditis indication.
Do not suppress palpitations empirically with rate-slowing drugs before rhythm and baseline conduction are understood.
counselling: Explain that MVP is common and often low risk; surveillance is based on regurgitation/severity and symptoms.
followUp: Track MR severity, symptoms and arrhythmia risk rather than the prolapse label alone.
examTrap: Giving antibiotic prophylaxis for routine dental work to every patient with MVP.
oneLinePearl: With MVP, the important question is not 'does it prolapse?' but 'does it leak or destabilize the heart?'.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart-valve disease resources

title: Severe Blood Pressure: Find Acute Organ Injury Before You Lower the Number
bottomLine: Hypertensive emergency is severe blood-pressure elevation with acute target-organ injury; the number alone does not define it. Recheck measurement properly, look for neurologic, cardiac, aortic, renal, retinal and pregnancy-related injury, and avoid rapid IV reduction when acute organ injury is absent.
recognize: Encephalopathy, focal deficit, pulmonary edema, ACS, aortic syndrome, AKI, retinal injury or severe pregnancy-related features indicate emergency physiology.
Pain, anxiety, missed medication and poor technique can cause marked BP elevation without acute target-organ injury.
differentiate: Severe asymptomatic hypertension generally needs confirmation, medication review and timely oral/outpatient management rather than rapid IV normalization.
Pregnancy/postpartum severe hypertension follows obstetric thresholds and medication pathways.
assessment: Repeat BP with correct cuff/technique and assess mental status, focal neurology, cardiopulmonary status, pulses, volume status and pregnancy/postpartum status.
Review stimulants/cocaine, NSAIDs, decongestants, MAOI/sympathomimetics and abrupt medication withdrawal.
workup: Order ECG/troponin, creatinine/electrolytes/urinalysis, imaging, fundoscopy or obstetric evaluation according to suspected organ injury—not one universal panel.
management: Emergency organ injury requires monitored syndrome-specific IV treatment and controlled reduction.
Without acute injury, address triggers, restart/intensify appropriate oral therapy and arrange close follow-up; avoid precipitous reduction.
medicationSafety: Overly rapid reduction can cause cerebral, coronary or renal hypoperfusion.
Medication choice depends on the emergency syndrome; aortic dissection, pulmonary edema and pregnancy do not use one interchangeable regimen.
counselling: Explain the difference between a high number and acute organ injury, while reinforcing long-term control.
followUp: For outpatient severe asymptomatic hypertension, arrange prompt BP/medication reassessment and access/adherence review.
examTrap: Using IV antihypertensive therapy to normalize an asymptomatic high BP without evidence of acute organ injury.
oneLinePearl: Hypertensive emergency is organ injury, not a scary number.

title: Cardiac Biomarkers: Injury, Strain, Trend, and Clinical Context
bottomLine: High-sensitivity troponin identifies myocardial injury, not its cause; BNP/NT-proBNP reflect cardiac wall stress, not heart failure by themselves. Acute interpretation requires serial change, ECG, symptoms, timing, renal function and the competing diagnoses that can raise the marker.
recognize: A rising/falling troponin pattern with ischemic evidence supports acute MI; stable chronic elevation can occur in CKD or structural heart disease.
BNP/NT-proBNP can rise with HF, AF, age, renal disease and pulmonary hypertension and can be lower in obesity.
differentiate: Sepsis, PE, myocarditis, tachyarrhythmia and severe hypertension can cause troponin-positive myocardial injury without type-1 plaque-rupture MI.
Normal natriuretic peptide values lower HF probability in the appropriate setting but should not overrule a strongly discordant clinical presentation.
assessment: Anchor biomarkers to onset/timing, ECG, hemodynamics, chest symptoms, HF signs, rhythm and renal function.
Ask what clinical decision the biomarker is intended to change before ordering it.
workup: Use the validated local serial high-sensitivity troponin algorithm and assay-specific thresholds.
Use BNP/NT-proBNP as an adjunct in dyspnea/HF assessment, not as a stand-alone diagnosis.
management: Treat the underlying syndrome: ACS, PE, sepsis, HF or myocarditis—not the laboratory number.
Escalate dynamic biomarker change with instability or ischemic ECG/symptoms through the acute cardiac pathway.
medicationSafety: Do not give ACS antithrombotics solely because troponin is elevated before evaluating competing causes and bleeding risk.
Avoid using CK-MB routinely when contemporary troponin answers myocardial-injury questions.
counselling: Explain that an elevated troponin means heart-muscle injury, but the cause still has to be identified.
followUp: Ensure abnormal biomarkers are linked to a final diagnosis and longitudinal plan rather than left as unexplained chart labels.
examTrap: Calling every elevated troponin an NSTEMI or every high BNP heart failure without the clinical syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Troponin says injury; BNP says strain; the patient tells you why.

title: ECG Interpretation: Rate, Rhythm, Axis, Intervals, Morphology, Ischemia, Then the Patient
bottomLine: Advanced ECG interpretation is a structured pattern-recognition task tied to clinical urgency. Confirm rate/rhythm, conduction intervals, QRS morphology/axis and ST-T changes, then decide whether the finding represents instability, ischemia, conduction disease, electrolyte/toxin effect or a benign variant.
recognize: Irregularly irregular rhythm requires electrocardiographic confirmation of AF rather than pulse impression alone.
Wide-complex tachycardia in an adult with structural disease should be treated as ventricular tachycardia until appropriately proven otherwise.
differentiate: ST elevation has ischemic and nonischemic mimics; reciprocal changes and clinical context matter.
QT prolongation risk depends on corrected QT, medications, electrolytes and bradycardia rather than one automated ECG label.
assessment: Assess symptoms/hemodynamics before completing a leisurely ECG analysis; unstable tachy/bradyarrhythmia is treated while the rhythm is identified.
Review medications, electrolytes, ischemic symptoms and prior ECG for comparison.
workup: Use serial ECGs and biomarkers for evolving ischemia, and telemetry/ambulatory monitoring for intermittent arrhythmia.
Verify machine interpretation manually when the decision is high stakes.
management: Activate emergency pathways for STEMI patterns, unstable tachy/bradyarrhythmia, high-grade block or malignant ventricular rhythm.
Use nonurgent referral/monitoring for stable conduction or ectopy findings according to symptoms/risk.
medicationSafety: Correct potassium/magnesium and avoid additive QT-prolonging drugs when clinically significant QT risk exists.
Do not treat sinus tachycardia with rate suppression before finding hemorrhage, sepsis, PE or other physiologic drivers.
counselling: Explain the practical significance rather than telling a patient they have an 'abnormal ECG' without context.
followUp: Close the loop on significant conduction, inherited-pattern or arrhythmia findings with cardiology/electrophysiology.
examTrap: Treating sinus tachycardia as SVT or accepting the automated ECG diagnosis without checking the tracing and patient.
oneLinePearl: ECG interpretation is structure first, urgency second, label last.

title: Cardiovascular Prevention: Treat Absolute Risk and High-Risk Conditions, Not One Number
bottomLine: Primary prevention integrates global cardiovascular risk, smoking, BP, diabetes, lipids, kidney disease, family history and patient preference; secondary prevention starts automatically after established ASCVD. The goal is risk reduction, not chasing isolated laboratory targets without context.
recognize: Established ASCVD, diabetes/CKD and markedly abnormal lipids can change treatment thresholds independently of a low short-term risk score.
Social determinants, medication cost and access materially affect prevention success.
differentiate: Primary prevention decisions are not identical to secondary prevention after MI/stroke/PAD.
Routine screening for asymptomatic CAD does not improve outcomes merely because risk factors exist; manage the risk factors directly unless symptoms/another indication arise.
assessment: Assess smoking, BP, lipids, diabetes, kidney disease, activity, diet, family history, pregnancy-related vascular history and established vascular disease.
Clarify medication tolerance, access and patient goals.
workup: Use Canadian risk estimation when applicable and identify statin-indicated/high-risk conditions.
Order additional imaging/biomarkers only when evidence shows they can refine a real decision.
management: Use smoking cessation, BP control, lipid therapy, diabetes/cardiorenal therapy, activity/nutrition and antithrombotic treatment where indicated.
Avoid routine aspirin for low-risk primary prevention when bleeding harm outweighs benefit.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic and lipid-lowering intensity must reflect benefit/risk, interactions and pregnancy considerations.
Do not abandon statin therapy after one symptom report without assessing causality and alternatives.
redFlags: High-risk diabetes/CKD without cardiorenal risk treatment
counselling: Discuss absolute benefit and barriers without blaming patients for risk factors; use shared decisions for preference-sensitive interventions.
followUp: Track BP, lipids, diabetes, smoking and adherence/access over time; prevention is longitudinal care.
examTrap: Ordering a stress test for an asymptomatic high-risk patient instead of aggressively managing risk factors.
oneLinePearl: Prevention treats risk; testing only helps when it changes that treatment.
sourceBasis: Hypertension Canada and Diabetes Canada risk-reduction guidance

title: Heart Failure Titration: Build Foundational Therapy, Then Monitor the Physiology It Changes
bottomLine: HF medication titration is not 'max one drug before starting the next.' For HFrEF, introduce foundational disease-modifying classes early as tolerated, then monitor BP, renal function, potassium, volume status, heart rate and adverse effects; HFnrEF uses phenotype/comorbidity-directed therapy rather than copying the HFrEF algorithm.
recognize: Worsening renal function or potassium after RAAS/MRA therapy needs context and repeat assessment, not automatic abandonment of all disease-modifying therapy.
Congestion and low-output/shock physiology require different medication decisions.
differentiate: Loop diuretics relieve congestion but are not substitutes for disease-modifying therapy.
HFnrEF with LVEF >40% has a different evidence base from HFrEF and should not be treated as 'normal EF no HF'.
assessment: Assess BP/orthostasis, HR/rhythm, weight/edema/JVP, renal function, potassium, symptoms, adherence/access and recent illness/NSAID use.
Identify frailty and goals that affect titration speed and tolerability.
workup: Check renal function/electrolytes after clinically meaningful RAAS/ARNI/MRA/diuretic changes and according to risk.
Use ECG/echo/iron and other testing when phenotype or therapy decision requires it.
management: For HFrEF, build ARNI/ACEi/ARB, evidence-based beta blocker, MRA and SGLT2-inhibitor therapy as tolerated rather than sequentially maximizing one class first.
Use diuretics to achieve euvolemia and specialist therapies/devices when indicated.
For HFnrEF, manage congestion and evidence-based comorbidity/phenotype therapies using current CCS guidance.
medicationSafety: Do not initiate/aggressively up-titrate beta blockade in cardiogenic shock or severe unstable decompensation.
Monitor potassium/renal function with RAAS/MRA therapy; SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/perioperative counselling.
counselling: Teach daily symptom/weight awareness, NSAID avoidance and when illness requires medication/sick-day review.
followUp: Titrate at planned intervals with labs/vitals and close the loop on HF clinic/device referral when appropriate.
examTrap: Waiting months to maximize one HFrEF drug before introducing other foundational classes—or stopping all RAAS therapy after a small creatinine change without context.
oneLinePearl: HF titration builds multiple foundations and monitors the physiology each one changes.

title: Pacemakers and ICDs: Pacing Treats Bradycardia; ICDs Treat Sudden-Death Risk
bottomLine: Pacemakers and ICDs solve different problems. Pacemakers address clinically important bradycardia/conduction disease; ICDs prevent sudden arrhythmic death in selected ventricular-arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy risk states. Device referral requires rhythm/EF/reversibility context—not a low heart rate or low EF alone.
recognize: Symptomatic high-grade AV block and selected sinus-node disease can require pacing.
Prior sustained VT/VF or selected persistent low-EF cardiomyopathy despite optimized therapy can create ICD indications.
differentiate: CRT is a resynchronization strategy for selected HF/conduction phenotypes and is not synonymous with a standard pacemaker.
A transient reversible bradyarrhythmia or newly diagnosed cardiomyopathy may not immediately justify permanent device implantation.
assessment: Assess syncope, rhythm documentation, reversible medication/electrolyte/ischemia causes, EF, QRS morphology/duration and duration of optimized HF therapy.
Review goals of care and competing comorbidity before ICD implantation/replacement decisions.
workup: Use ECG/monitoring/echo and electrophysiology or specialist evaluation according to the indication.
Interrogate existing devices when shocks, syncope, pacing failure or lead/battery concern occurs.
management: Urgently pace unstable bradycardia through the acute algorithm when indicated.
Refer qualifying patients for permanent pacemaker, ICD or CRT consideration after reversible causes and guideline timing are addressed.
medicationSafety: Rate-slowing drugs can worsen brady/conduction disease and should be reviewed.
Inappropriate ICD shocks can result from arrhythmia/device issues and require device-clinic evaluation rather than repeated sedative prescribing.
counselling: Teach what the device does, what a shock means, wound/infection signs and driving/activity restrictions using current Canadian guidance.
followUp: Ensure device-clinic/remote monitoring, HF optimization and shock/syncope follow-up are closed-loop.
examTrap: Assuming an ICD is a treatment for any EF below normal or that a pacemaker prevents ventricular tachycardia.
oneLinePearl: Pacemaker = brady/conduction support; ICD = sudden-death protection; CRT = selected resynchronization.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/CHRS device and heart-failure resources

title: Endocarditis Prevention: Prophylaxis Is for Specific Highest-Risk Hearts and Procedures
bottomLine: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not for every murmur, MVP or valve lesion. Reserve it for the highest-risk cardiac conditions undergoing procedures where current guidance recommends prophylaxis; otherwise emphasize oral health, aseptic technique and prompt evaluation of possible endocarditis.
recognize: Highest-risk groups include selected prosthetic-valve/material, prior infective endocarditis and specific congenital/other high-risk conditions according to current guidance.
Fever plus new murmur, embolic phenomena, prosthetic valve/device or bacteremia risk requires diagnostic endocarditis evaluation—not a prophylaxis prescription.
differentiate: Dental prophylaxis prevention is different from treatment of active bacteremia/endocarditis.
Routine GI/GU procedures generally do not trigger prophylaxis solely because valve disease exists unless another active-infection indication applies.
assessment: Confirm the exact cardiac condition/prosthetic material, prior endocarditis and planned procedure.
Review allergy history before selecting any recommended prophylactic antibiotic.
workup: No testing is required merely to give prophylaxis; suspected endocarditis requires blood cultures and echocardiographic/infectious-disease evaluation.
management: Use current Canadian/AHA-endorsed highest-risk prophylaxis criteria and procedure-specific regimens where applicable.
Promote routine dental care and address active oral infection rather than relying on episodic antibiotics.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics because allergy, C. difficile and resistance harms exceed benefit in low-risk patients.
Do not give prophylaxis instead of obtaining blood cultures first when active endocarditis is suspected.
counselling: Explain why prophylaxis is intentionally limited to highest-risk situations and why oral health is important prevention.
followUp: Document the specific indication so future clinicians do not expand or omit prophylaxis inappropriately.
examTrap: Giving prophylactic antibiotics to every patient with a heart murmur or MVP before dental cleaning.
oneLinePearl: Endocarditis prophylaxis is narrow by design: highest-risk heart, qualifying procedure.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society heart-valve disease resources
